questions.q: Thomson had already measured the electron's charge-to-mass ratio. Why did this NOT tell physicists the charge of a single electron?
options: His apparatus was too crude to read the numbers off the screen
A ratio ties two unknowns together, so knowing charge divided by mass still leaves both the charge and the mass unknown
He measured the mass directly but never the charge
Cathode rays turned out not to be electrons after all
questions.explanation: Thomson measured charge ÷ mass, but a single ratio is two unknowns tangled together: if some number divided by another equals ten, you still know neither. Measuring the charge by itself was needed to untangle them — and would hand you the electron's mass as a bonus.

questions.q: Millikan's early attempts used water droplets and kept failing. What change, suggested by graduate student Harvey Fletcher, fixed the problem?
options: Cooling the chamber so the droplets would not move
Switching from water to oil, which evaporates so slowly that a droplet can be watched for hours instead of seconds
Using a much stronger electric field to hold the droplets still
Replacing the telescope with a more powerful microscope
questions.explanation: Water droplets a few millionths of a metre across evaporated and vanished within minutes or seconds. Fletcher proposed clock oil, which evaporates so slowly a single droplet could be observed for hours — the practical fix that made the experiment possible.

questions.q: How did Millikan determine the mass of a droplet he could barely see and never put on a scale?
options: He weighed thousands of droplets together and divided by the count
He turned the field off, let the droplet fall at its terminal velocity, and used Stokes's law (with the air's viscosity and the oil's density) to find its radius and hence its mass
He measured how brightly the droplet glittered under the side lighting
He read the mass directly from the voltage needed to hold it still
questions.explanation: With the field off, the tiny droplet quickly reaches a constant terminal velocity where air drag balances its weight. Timing its fall over a fixed distance and applying Stokes's law (knowing the air's viscosity and the oil's density) gives the radius, then the volume, then the mass — weighing it by watching how fast it falls.

questions.q: When the droplet hangs motionless (or moves at constant velocity) between the plates, which relationship does an examiner want you to set up to solve for the charge?
options: Weight equals air resistance, so \(mg = 6\pi\eta r v\)
The downward weight equals the upward electric force, so \(mg = qE = qV/d\), giving \(q = mgd/V\)
The electric force equals the drag force, so \(qE = 6\pi\eta r v\)
Charge equals voltage times plate separation, so \(q = Vd\)
questions.explanation: At balance the net force is zero: the upward electric force (field strength × charge, with field = voltage ÷ plate separation) equals the downward weight (mass × gravity). Rearranging \(mg = qV/d\) gives \(q = mgd/V\), where every quantity on the right was measured.

questions.q: Measuring one droplet gives the total charge of all the electrons stuck to it. How did Millikan extract the charge of a SINGLE electron from hundreds of such measurements?
options: He averaged all the droplet charges together
He found that every measured charge was a whole-number multiple of one tiny value, and identified that indivisible unit as the elementary charge
He picked the smallest droplet charge he ever recorded
He divided each droplet's charge by the number of droplets
questions.explanation: Across hundreds of droplets the charges were never random — always a clean whole-number multiple of one fundamental amount (two, eight, eighteen electrons' worth, never two-and-a-half). That common indivisible unit is the charge on a single electron, the quantum of charge.

questions.q: What did the X-ray gun let Millikan do that made his proof of quantised charge decisive rather than merely suggestive?
options: It lit the droplets so they could be seen against the dark background
It ionised the air so a single droplet could gain or lose electrons mid-experiment, and the charge always jumped by a whole-number multiple of the same unit
It heated the oil so the droplets evaporated on command
It measured the droplet's charge directly without needing the voltage
questions.explanation: Firing X-rays ionised the gas, letting a single droplet pick up or lose electrons while Millikan watched. Re-balancing and re-measuring, he saw the charge change one electron at a time — always by a clean whole-number of the same fundamental lump, never a fraction.

questions.q: From memory: outline the two stages by which Millikan measured the charge on a droplet, and state the result the experiment established.
keyPoints: Stage 1 – weigh the droplet: turn the field off, let it fall at terminal velocity, and use Stokes's law (air viscosity, oil density) to get the radius, hence the mass.
Stage 2 – find the charge: turn the field on and balance the droplet so the upward electric force equals the weight, then solve \(q = mgd/V\).
Result: the fundamental charge is about \(1.6\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}\), and electric charge is quantised – it comes only in whole-number multiples of that unit.
questions.explanation: If you recalled both stages (terminal-velocity weighing, then force balance for the charge) and the quantisation conclusion, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: explain the 'cautionary tale' Richard Feynman drew from the years of measurements after Millikan — why did later values of the electron's charge creep slowly upward rather than scatter randomly?
keyPoints: Later measurements climbed gradually toward the modern (higher) value instead of scattering around it from the start.
When a scientist got a value far from Millikan's, they assumed something was wrong and hunted for the error until the number came down; when close to Millikan's, they stopped looking.
So errors pushing away from Millikan were caught while errors keeping it near were left — the field was unconsciously dragged toward his slightly wrong answer.
Feynman's lesson: the hardest person to keep honest in science is yourself — the answer you expect can bend the answer you find.
questions.explanation: The point is experimenter bias, not fraud: knowing the expected answer made scientists scrutinise only the inconvenient results. Recall the asymmetric error-hunting and Feynman's warning to grade Good or Easy.

questions.q: Millikan's 1913 paper reported the elementary charge as \(1.592\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}\). The modern defined value is \(1.602\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{C}\). Find the percentage by which Millikan's value falls short of the modern one.
working: \(\approx 0.62\%\) — about six-tenths of one percent, as the episode states.
questions.explanation: The tiny shortfall — roughly 0.6% — came almost entirely from a slightly wrong published value for the viscosity of air, which fed straight into the droplet-radius calculation. Fix that one constant and his result snaps onto the modern value.

questions.q: Holton's study of the notebooks found Millikan published data from 58 droplets but had actually recorded about 175. What fraction (as a percentage) of his measured droplets did he report?
working: \(\approx 33\%\) — about a third, meaning roughly two-thirds were left out.
questions.explanation: Reporting only about a third of the droplets, while the paper claimed the result rested on 'all of the drops experimented upon', is the data-selection controversy. Notably, Franklin showed that adding all 175 back in barely changes the final value.
